554.title: Not ten thousand years
554.hook: don't act as if you'll live ten thousand years; while you can, be good (Meditations 4.17)
554.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius use Meditations 4.17 as a prompt to stop postponing small kindnesses.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Marcus, taking away the opinion. Your line was take away the label.

Ten thousand years. That's the number Marcus Aurelius chose, and it's meant to be absurd. Nobody plans on living that long. And yet a thank-you waits a season, then a year. An apology stays ready in the head and never reaches the mouth. A visit to an aunt who keeps saying come anytime slides to some later month, as though later were endless. In book four Marcus wrote himself a reminder short enough for a sticky note. Today: not ten thousand years.
screen: `TEN THOUSAND YEARS.` → `AS THOUGH LATER WERE ENDLESS.` → `NOT TEN THOUSAND YEARS.`

segments.voice: In George Long's 1862 translation, the seventeenth entry reads: "Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good." A warning, a fact, and an instruction. Ten thousand years is the joke inside the warning. Marcus isn't accusing himself of a belief. He's accusing himself of a habit: putting off the good because there always seems to be more time. Death hangs over you. He doesn't say it to frighten himself. Stoic writers kept death in view on purpose, as a way of sorting what matters from what doesn't. If this might be the last week, the thank-you note moves up, and the argument about the thermostat moves down. Then: while you can, be good. Notice he doesn't say be productive, or be famous, or finish your list. He says be good. And he puts a condition on it: while it is in your power. Not when you're less busy. Not when the kids are grown. Not when you've earned a rest. The good you've been saving isn't kept somewhere safe. It's quietly expiring. Is later actually promised? Marcus's answer, in three short sentences, was no.

555.title: Time gained
555.hook: how much time you gain by not watching what your neighbor says or does (Meditations 4.18)
555.carry: run straight along the line, without swerving
555.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes practice Meditations 4.18 by skipping one habit of checking on others, such as a feed, and spending the time on their own work.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was George Long, whose translation says don't act as if you had ten thousand years. Your line was be good while I can.

A woman stands at her kitchen window, coffee going cold. Across the street, the neighbors have a new car. She notices the color, guesses the price, wonders how they afford it, remembers what her sister said about them, then checks the clock. Twenty minutes, gone, on a life that isn't hers. Marcus Aurelius knew the habit long before anyone carried a window onto other lives in their pocket. And he did the accounting. Today: time gained.

segments.voice: How much leisure he gains, Marcus writes in the eighteenth entry of book four, who doesn't look to see what his neighbor says or does or thinks, but only at what he himself is doing, so that it may be just and holy. The Greek word is euscholia, good leisure: time that's free. Watching others spends it. Marcus isn't saying ignore people or stop caring. He's saying stop monitoring: checking what others are up to so you can compare, judge, or feel better or worse. It costs time, and buys almost nothing you can use. The attention you take back goes to one question: is what I'm doing just? A carpenter looking at the next bench all day doesn't build a better chair. Then an image from the racetrack. Don't look around at the dark character of others, he says, but run straight along the line, without swerving. A runner who keeps glancing sideways loses ground. Some of the time we wish we had may already be in the day, leaking out sideways into other people's cars and kitchens and arguments. Close that leak, even partly, and the minutes come back.

556.title: Fame forgets
556.hook: everyone who remembers you will soon die too (Meditations 4.19)
556.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes answer Meditations 4.19 with anonymous acts: a good deed done so that no one will know who did it.

segments.voice: Name your great-grandparents. All eight of them, without looking anything up. These were people who worked, loved, worried about money, told jokes at dinner, and were, for a while, the center of somebody's world. Three generations on, some of their names have slipped even from their own family. Marcus Aurelius, whose face was stamped on coins across an empire, did that same arithmetic about himself, and used it to loosen the grip of wanting to be remembered. Today: fame forgets.

segments.voice: In the nineteenth entry of book four Marcus writes about the person who longs to be remembered after death. They don't stop to think, he says, that every one of those who remember them will soon die too, and then those who come after, until the whole memory goes out, passed from one person to the next, through people who admire and then die. Then he pushes further. Suppose the people who remember you were immortal, and the memory too. What would that be to you? You'd be gone. Praise can't reach the dead. And to the living, he asks, what is praise, except for some practical use? Information, at best. It doesn't make the act better or worse. So what's left is the act itself. Do good to be remembered, and you're building on something that will dissolve. Do it because it's good, and it's complete the moment it's done. This can sound bleak. But look at the questions it answers: will anyone notice, will this count, will they know it was me? Marcus sets them down. In the end, nobody will remember. So the good thing can be done without an audience, the way a great-grandmother might once have fed a neighbor's child and never written it down. Her name may be gone. The meal was still eaten.

557.title: The emerald
557.hook: is an emerald worse if no one praises it? (Meditations 4.20)
557.carry: an honest answer in an empty room
557.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes recall the emerald of Meditations 4.20 after doing something good, letting it stand without checking for anyone's reaction.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was fame forgets. Your line was no credit: a good act is complete without it.

Deep in a mountain in Colombia, there's an emerald nobody has found. It has been green for millions of years in the dark. No jeweler has held it to the light. No one has said, oh, look at that. Is it any less green? Marcus Aurelius asked almost exactly that question, in the entry right after the one on fame. Yesterday was about being remembered. This one is quieter: whether a good thing needs to be seen at all. Today: the emerald.
screen: `AN EMERALD NOBODY HAS FOUND.` → `IS IT ANY LESS GREEN?` → `THE EMERALD.`

segments.voice: Everything beautiful, Marcus writes in the twentieth entry of book four, is beautiful on its own, and complete in itself. Praise is no part of it. A thing isn't made worse or better by being praised. Then he gets wonderfully specific. Is an emerald made worse, he asks, if it isn't praised? What about gold, or ivory, or purple dye? A lyre? A small knife? A flower? A shrub? You can almost picture him glancing around the room. None of these changes color when someone walks past without comment. That holds for objects and works of art, he says, and even more for what is truly beautiful: law, truth, kindness, modesty. Which of these is beautiful because it's praised, or spoiled because it's blamed? An honest answer given in an empty room is just as honest. A kindness nobody saw is just as kind. After doing something good, it's easy to wait a little for the reaction: the text back, the thank-you, the like. When it doesn't come, the good thing seems to dim. Marcus says it didn't dim. It was finished, and green, and whole, before anyone looked. That's not an argument against thanking people. Gratitude is a good of its own. It's an argument against needing it, against letting the value of your work sit in someone else's hands.

558.title: Do less
558.hook: to be at peace, do few things, and only what's necessary (Meditations 4.24)
558.carry: ask who actually needs me now
558.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use the question from Meditations 4.24, 'is this one of the unnecessary things?', to trim their lists and their replies.

segments.voice: Look at your to-do list. Not the written one, the one in your head. Reply to that. Look into this. Weigh in on the group chat. Have an opinion about the news. Check the thing you already checked. It's long, and it's hard to say which items actually matter. Marcus Aurelius had more on his plate than most, and in the twenty-fourth entry of book four he passed on an old piece of advice that sounds almost like permission. Today: do less.

segments.voice: Do few things, says the philosopher, if you want to be at peace. Marcus doesn't name him. Readers usually identify him as Democritus, an earlier Greek thinker who wrote about cheerful calm. Then Marcus improves it. Wouldn't it be better, he asks, to say: do what's necessary, and what the reason of a social creature requires, and in the way it requires? That brings a double peace: the peace of doing things well, and the peace of doing few. Not just fewer. Fewer and better. Then the hard sentence. Most of what we say and do, Marcus writes, isn't necessary. Take it away, and you'll have more leisure and less disturbance. So at every moment, ask: is this one of the unnecessary things? And he goes a step deeper. Cut the unnecessary thoughts, he says, and the unnecessary actions that follow them won't happen either. The extra reply starts as an extra thought. The extra worry starts as one more what-if. This isn't laziness. It's triage. A doctor in a crowded room doesn't treat everyone at once; she asks who actually needs her now. Do less isn't a mood. It's a question, asked often, with an honest answer.

559.title: The time of Vespasian
559.hook: picture Vespasian's age: marrying, farming, flattering, all gone (Meditations 4.32)
559.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes picture their own town a century ago, as in Meditations 4.32, to see their present worries at their true size.

segments.voice: Yesterday: do less, only what's necessary. Your line was ask who actually needs me now.

Find an old photograph of your street from about a hundred years ago. A man in a hat hurrying somewhere. Two women talking outside a shop. A boy with a bicycle. Each of them was in the middle of something urgent: a debt, a crush, a quarrel with a brother. Every one of those urgencies is finished now. Marcus Aurelius did this exercise without photographs, using an emperor from an earlier generation of Rome.

segments.voice: Think of the times of Vespasian, Marcus writes in book four, entry thirty-two. Vespasian was an emperor from before Marcus's time. And what do you see? People marrying, raising children, getting sick, dying, fighting wars, feasting, trading, farming, flattering, being stubbornly proud, suspecting, plotting, wishing others dead, grumbling at the present, loving, piling up treasure, longing for high office and for power. Everything people did then, and do now. And that whole life of theirs, Marcus says, no longer exists anywhere. Then he does it again with the emperor Trajan's time, a little closer. Same list. Also gone. He isn't doing this to feel gloomy or superior. He's doing it to measure. The quarrel that feels enormous this week is the same size as the quarrels in Vespasian's Rome. Look, he says, at how many threw themselves into these things, and then fell, and came apart. What lasts, for him, is not the outcome of the hurry. It's whether, in the middle of it, a person kept to what is right. The exercise shrinks the hurry, not the good. The worries get smaller. Character doesn't.

560.hook: be like the headland the waves break on; it stands, and the water settles (Meditations 4.49)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Vespasian, whose whole busy age is gone. Your line was all gone.

Stand on a rocky point in a storm. Gray waves come one after another and hit the rock with a sound like a slammed door. Spray flies up and falls back. The water slides away, foaming, and goes quiet in the cove behind the point. The rock hasn't moved. It hasn't fought. It just stood there, and the sea calmed itself around it. Marcus Aurelius saw that picture and kept it.
screen: `A ROCKY POINT IN A STORM.` → `THE ROCK HASN'T MOVED.` → `THE HEADLAND.`

segments.voice: Book four, entry forty-nine, in George Long's 1862 translation: "Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it." A promontory is a headland: high land running out into the sea. Notice continually. The waves don't stop because the rock is steady. Marcus isn't promising a life without trouble; he expects the waves. And the rock doesn't attack the sea or argue with it. By staying where it is, it gives the water nothing to push against, and the fury spends itself and falls quiet. The angry customer, the relative on the phone, the news crashing in all morning: the headland doesn't break them. It just doesn't move. Now look back at this week. Be good while I can: don't save the good for later. Time gained: stop monitoring others. No credit: do good without an audience. The emerald: what's good is whole unpraised. Do less: only what's necessary. All gone: Vespasian's Rome. Each one sets down a weight: later, comparison, credit, praise, busyness, urgency. What's left is something like a rock in the sea. Not hard. Just steady.
screen: `BE LIKE THE PROMONTORY.` · `THE WAVES BREAK CONTINUALLY.` · `IT STANDS, AND THE WATER SETTLES.` · `A WEEK OF WEIGHTS SET DOWN.` · then, large: `THE HEADLAND.`

segments.voice: Sit like a headland: feet heavy, back tall, shoulders loose. Let one frustration from this week come in like a wave, notice the spray and the urge to push back, and don't move. Breathe, and watch it slide away; if another comes, let it break too.
The headland. Marcus says be like the promontory the waves keep breaking on: it stands firm, and the water calms around it. Today's word.
Your line: spray flies up and falls back. The rock stays; the water settles. Day five hundred sixty, a week well spent.
